title: Master Class | Sicilian Defence, Smith–Morra Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The cleanest way to meet this gambit is to decline it — accepting the pawn is playable but dangerous, since the defender has to know a great deal to survive, which is exactly the fight the gambiteer wants.
The best declining move is the knight to f6 — developing and counterattacking the central pawn at once, which forces the opponent into a tamer, transposed structure rather than the sharp main lines.

Since the opponent declined to push the centre, now the pawn can be safely taken — and it's a superior version, because the bishop parked on d3 is passive, staring into its own pawn instead of raking toward the king. That single misplacement drains most of the activity the gambit is supposed to buy.

The tempting central push would weaken the d5 square, letting the opponent trade off a knight and plant a piece on the outpost. So begin with a flexible developing move, the knight to c6, with a modest pawn move to follow.

The pawn to d6 stops the central advance — and note how much friendlier this is than a real Morra, where the attacking bishop and an open file give the aggressor real chances. Here, everything is under control.

There's the eternal debate between the restrained and the fianchetto setups — and the deciding factor is urgency. With no pressure on development, there's time to optimise the bishop onto the long diagonal, since the central break isn't available to the opponent anyway.

The pin doesn't actually threaten the knight, so there's no need to react to it — the real question is whether to insert a rook-pawn move. Follow the logic: castling invites the standard plan of trading off the fianchettoed bishop, which would leave lasting holes around the king.

That bishop is the strongest piece on the board, so preserve it — the rook-pawn nudge, played while the rook is still home, shoos the bishop off the key diagonal. Then castling becomes safe, with the trade-off idea defused.

And here's the resource that makes the whole plan hold together — a king step to h7. It shores up the weakened pawn, and without it the earlier rook-pawn move simply wouldn't work. The king is perfectly safe there, screened by its own pawn chain.

Don't lash out with the central push, which would blunt the fianchettoed bishop and weaken d5 again. Instead solve the other bishop's development by bringing it to e6 — usually a square to avoid, but when the bishop isn't hemmed in it's an excellent, centralising post that controls the key square.

In a solid position like this, don't force matters — improve in measured steps. When you're unsure how to make progress, tap the pool of reasonable improving moves rather than freezing up. A rook to c8 activates the piece and contests the file — not every move has to climb Mount Everest.

A lovely little regrouping — a knight back to d7. It lifts the knight toward e5 or c5, reopens the bishop's diagonal, covers a central square, and readies the knight for an outpost. Small, substantive actions that quietly make the whole position healthier.

As the opponent reroutes a knight toward an outpost, adapt — one knight jump risks a pawn, so instead the knight leaps to e5. It seems to block the bishop again, but only for a moment: from e5 it either takes an important bishop or hops on to a dominant square.

The capture leaves the opponent in a bind — move the bishop and a knight to c4 is crushing. The rook-pawn that looks loose is left hanging by design; it's not really lost, and even if it were, it's the least of the pawns to give. The opponent must either shed the strong bishop, ending all attacking hopes, or permit the knight to that monster square.

When there's a choice of recaptures, make the positionally conscious one — take with the bishop, not the queen. Recapturing with the queen would allow a rook to the open file with tempo; keeping the file uncontested is worth more than the small material nicety.

A concept many players miss — an exposed queen isn't only something to attack with pieces or try to trap; it can be 'attacked' by your own queen to force a trade you actually want. Up a pawn and craving the open file, offering that swap hits the bishop and the queen at once, forcing the exchange into total queenside domination for the endgame.
